![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14156042/assets/e00b5083b25408240fb0eef26c898e237437bf9fe0f7fce11e397b9d7683a1c2.png)

The figure above shows the graph of a piecewise linear function $y=f(x).$ The point $A$ has coordinates $(2,0)$ and lies on $y=f(x).$ Given that $(0,2)$ lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x),$ what is $({f}^{-1})^{′}(0)?$

$({f}^{-1})^{′}(0)=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
Since $(0,2)$ lies on ${f}^{-1},$ we have ${f}^{-1}(0)=2.$ 
The slope of the tangent to $f(x)$ for $x\in [0,4]$ is $\frac{1}{2}$, hence, ${f}^{′}(2)=\frac{1}{2}.$

The formula for the derivative of the inverse function is 

$$
({f}^{-1})^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(x))}.
$$

Evaluating at $x=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(0) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(0))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{2})} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the function $f(x)=\frac{1}{3}{x}^{2}+4x+10$ and the point $P(0,10)$ that lies on $y=f(x).$ Given that $f(x)$ is invertible in the vicinity of $P,$ determine the slope of $y={f}^{-1}(x)$ at the point $(10,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
We start by calculating the derivative of $f$ at the point $(0,10).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{1}{3}{x}^{2}+4x+10 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{2}{3}x+4 \\ {f}^{′}(0) & =4\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(0,10)$ lies on $y=f(x),$ we know that the corresponding point $(10,0)$ lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x).$

Furthermore, the slopes of the tangents to the two respective points are reciprocals. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(10) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(10))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(0)} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

We start by calculating the derivative of $f$ at the point $(\frac{\pi }{6},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}).$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{6}) & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\ {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{6}) & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{6}) & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(\frac{\pi }{6},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})$ lies on $y=f(x),$ we know that the corresponding point $(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{\pi }{6})$ lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x).$

Furthermore, the slopes of the tangents to the two respective points are reciprocals. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{6})} \\  & =\frac{1}{(\frac{3}{2})} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(1)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(1))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(1).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(1)=x.$ For $x>\frac{1}{2},$ this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(1) & =x \\ f(x) & =1 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2x-1}} & =1 \\ 1 & =\sqrt{2x-1} \\ 1 & =2x-1 \\ x & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{-1}(1)=1.$

Now, we calculate ${f}^{′}(1),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2x-1}} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\frac{1}{(2x-1)^{3/2}} \\ {f}^{′}(1) & =-\frac{1}{(2\cdot 1-1)^{3/2}} \\ {f}^{′}(1) & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(1) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(1))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(1)} \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(0),$ we use the following formula:

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(0)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(0))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(0).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(0)=x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(0) & =x \\ f(x) & =0 \\ (x+3)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1) & =0 \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{-1}(0)=2.$

Now, we calculate ${f}^{′}(2),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(x+3)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1) \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1)+\frac{x+3}{x-1} \\ {f}^{′}(2) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2-1)+\frac{2+3}{2-1} \\ {f}^{′}(2) & =0+5 \\ {f}^{′}(2) & =5\end{aligned}

$$

questions.problem: Consider the function $f(x)={2}^{x}+1.$ Given that $y=f(x)$ is invertible throughout its domain, determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(5).$
questions.worked_solution:
To determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(5),$ we use the following formula:

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(5)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(5))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(5).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(5)=x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(5) & =x \\ f(x) & =5 \\ {2}^{x}+1 & =5 \\ {2}^{x} & =4 \\ {2}^{x} & ={2}^{2} \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{-1}(5)=2.$

Now, we calculate ${f}^{′}(2),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={2}^{x}+1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2\cdot {2}^{x} \\ {f}^{′}(2) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2\cdot {2}^{2} \\ {f}^{′}(2) & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(5) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(5))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the function $f(x)=3x+\sqrt{x}.$ Given that $y=f(x)$ is invertible throughout its domain, determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(2).$
questions.worked_solution:
To determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(2),$ we use the following formula:

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(2)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(2))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(2).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(2)=x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(2) & =x \\ f(x) & =2 \\ 3x+\sqrt{x} & =2 \\ \sqrt{x} & =2-3x \\ x & =4-12x+9{x}^{2} \\ 9{x}^{2}-13x+4 & =0 \\ (9x-4)(x-1) & =0 \\ x & =\frac{4}{9},\,1.\end{aligned}
$$

Checking the solutions, we notice that only $x=\frac{4}{9}$ satisfies the equation $3x+\sqrt{x}=2.$ Therefore, we discard $x=1$ and conclude that ${f}^{-1}(2)=\frac{4}{9}.$

Now, we calculate ${f}^{′}(\frac{4}{9}),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =3x+\sqrt{x} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =3+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} \\ {f}^{′}(\frac{4}{9}) & =3+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{(\frac{4}{9})}} \\ {f}^{′}(\frac{4}{9}) & =3+\frac{3}{4} \\ {f}^{′}(\frac{4}{9}) & =\frac{15}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(1) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(1))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(\frac{4}{9})} \\  & =\frac{4}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the function $f(x)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-4).$ Given that $y=f(x)$ is invertible throughout its domain, determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(0).$
questions.worked_solution:
To determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(0),$ we use the following formula:

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(0)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(0))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(0).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(0)=x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(0) & =x \\ f(x) & =0 \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-4) & =0 \\ x & =0,\,5.\end{aligned}
$$

We discard $x=0$ since the logarithm is not defined here. Therefore, ${f}^{-1}(0)=5.$

Now, we calculate ${f}^{′}(5),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-4) \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-4)+\frac{x}{x-4} \\ {f}^{′}(5) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5-4)+\frac{5}{5-4} \\ {f}^{′}(5) & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(0) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(0))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(5)} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Example: 
                    Calculating the Derivative of an Inverse Function From a Graph
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14156042/assets/8fb287885c948b7e563b5fa878dd204dacbedea311490c4573aa883bff992662.png)

The figure above shows the graph of a function $y=f(x)$ and its inverse $y=f^{-1}(x).$ The point $A$ has coordinates $(2, 0)$ and lies on $y=f(x).$
The point $B$ has coordinates $(0,2)$ and lies on $y=f^{-1}(x).$ If $f'(2)=-\dfrac{3}{2},$ what is $(f^{-1})'(0)?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since $B \,(0,2)$ lies on $f^{-1},$ we have $f^{-1}(0) = 2.$ We're also told that $f'(2)=-\dfrac{3}{2}.$

The formula for the derivative of the inverse function is

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(x))}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(0) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(0))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-\frac{3}{2})} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Example: 
                    Calculating the Derivative of an Inverse Function
canonical_examples.problem: Consider the function $f(x) = \dfrac{2-3x}{4+5x}$ and the point $P\left(-1,-5\right)$ that lies on $y=f(x).$ Given that $f(x)$ is invertible in the vicinity of $P,$ determine the slope of $y=f^{-1}(x)$ at the point $\left(-5,-1\right).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We start by calculating the derivative of $f$ at the point $(-1, -5).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{2-3x}{4+5x} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\frac{22}{(4+5x)^{2}} \\ {f}^{′}(-1) & =-22\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(-1, -5)$ lies on $y=f(x),$ we know that the corresponding point $(-5, -1)$ lies on $y=f^{-1}(x).$ 

Furthermore, the slopes of the tangents to the two respective points are reciprocals. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(-5) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(-5))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(-1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-22)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{22}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Calculating the Derivative of an Inverse Function Using a Table
canonical_examples.problem:
The following table gives the values of $f(x), f'(x),g(x),$ and $g'(x)$ at some points. Find $(f^{-1}\cdot g)'(1)$ of the product of functions.

| **$x$** | $f(x)$ | $f'(x)$ | $g(x)$ | $g'(x)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $-1$ | $2$ | $-3$ | $1$ |
| $2$ | $1$ | $-1$ | $3$ | $5$ |
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The formula for the derivative of the inverse $f^{-1}(x)$ is

$$
(f^{-1})'(x) = \dfrac{1}{f'(f^{-1}(x))}.
$$

Using this, and the product rule, the derivative of the function $f^{-1}(x)g(x)$ is

$$
(f^{-1}\cdot g)'(x)=\dfrac{g(x)}{f'(f^{-1}(x))}+g'(x)f^{-1}(x).
$$

Substituting $x=1,$ we have

$$
(f^{-1}\cdot g)'(1) =\dfrac{g(1)}{f'(f^{-1}(1))}+g'(1)f^{-1}(1).
$$

From the table, we obtain $f^{-1}(1)=2,$ $g(1)=-3,$ $g'(1)=1,$ and $f'(2)=-1.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1}\cdot g)^{′}(1) & =\frac{g(1)}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(1))}+{g}^{′}(1){f}^{-1}(1) \\  & =\frac{-3}{{f}^{′}(2)}+1\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{-3}{-1}+2 \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Consider the function $f(x) =3e^{x}-1.$ Given that $y = f(x)$ is invertible throughout its domain, determine $(f^{-1})'(2).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To determine $(f^{-1})'(2),$ we use the following formula:

$$
\left(f^{-1}\right)'(2) = \dfrac{1}{f'(f^{-1}(2))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of $f^{-1}(2).$ To do this, we solve the equation $f^{-1}(2) = x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(2) & =x \\ f(x) & =2 \\ 3{e}^{x}-1 & =2 \\ 3{e}^{x} & =3 \\ {e}^{x} & =1 \\ x & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f^{-1}(2) = 0.$

Now, we calculate $f'(0),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =3{e}^{x}-1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =3{e}^{x} \\ {f}^{′}(0) & =3{e}^{0} \\ {f}^{′}(0) & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(2) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(2))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(0)} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Consider the following function: 

$$
f(x)= 4x^2+x, \qquad x \gt 0
$$

The domain restriction $x > 0$ means that $f$ is invertible on its entire domain. 

The point $P$ with coordinates $(2,18)$ lies on the curve $y = f(x).$ This means that the point $P'$ with coordinates $(18,2)$ lies on the curve of the inverse function $y=f^{-1}(x),$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14156042/assets/3e16e532743be547c766e5a6a47bae8933a8dedb2b6d0fa0d60d47cc0b37ba04.png)

How do we find $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}$ at the point $P'?$

For this, we will use the fact that the slope of the tangent to the curve $y=f^{-1}(x)$ at $P'$ is the *reciprocal* of the slope of the tangent to the curve $y=f(x)$ at $P.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{{P}^{′}}=\frac{1}{({\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{P})}\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}$ at $P$ is straightforward. First, we differentiate $y=f(x).$ This gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}  = 8x + 1,
$$

and then plugging in $x=2$ gives

$$
\left.\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}\right|_P = 8(2)+1 = 17.
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\left.\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}\right|_{P'}= \dfrac{1}{17}
$$

We can summarize this process using the following formula:

$$
\left(f^{-1}\right)'(x) = \dfrac{1}{f'(f^{-1}(x))}
$$

To help remember this formula, note that it's okay to swap the derivative symbol (the prime) with the inverse symbol (the exponent of $-1$) as long as we take the reciprocal afterward.

tutorials.name: Calculating Derivatives Using Tables
tutorials.problem:
The following table gives the values of functions $f(x)$ and $f'(x)$ at some points. 

| **$x$** | $f(x)$ | $f'(x)$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $2$ | $3$ |
| $2$ | $1$ | $12$ |

Let's use this data to find $(f^{-1})'(1).$ 

Recall that the formula for the derivative of the inverse is

$$
(f^{-1})'(x) = \dfrac{1}{f'(f^{-1}(x))}.
$$

Substituting $x=1,$ we have

$$
(f^{-1})'(1) = \dfrac{1}{f'(f^{-1}(1))}.
$$

From the table, we see that $f(2)=1$, hence $f^{-1}(1)=2$, and also $f'(2)=12$. Therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(1) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(1))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can also use the rule for calculating derivatives of inverse functions in conjunction with other rules of differentiation. Let's see an example.
